claude.sample_unit: radiology reports (CT and MRI), each transformed into 17 reading-grade versions

links.outcome: Accuracy and potential management-altering errors of LLM reports simplified to low reading grade levels
links.effect: Accuracy declined significantly below grade 11; at 7th-grade level 20% (20/100) of reports had potential changes in patient management (generalization 8/20, omission 7/20, incorrect conversion 7/20).
links.quote: Among the 100 reports transformed to a 7th-grade reading level, 20% (20/100) exhibited potential changes in patient management when compared to the original reports.

links.outcome: Consistency of LLM output accuracy across equivalent prompts varying in requested literacy level
links.effect: Accuracy plateaued at grades 13-17 (median total score 15) but dropped significantly below grade 11; level 10 vs 13 accurate-report proportions 0.97 vs 0.89 (radiologists) and 0.95 vs 0.68 (PubMed-BERTScore).
links.quote: When investigating the statistical significance of the proportion of accurate reports in descending order from reading grade level 13, the first level to show a significant difference was level 10 for both the total accuracy score assigned by radiologists (Fig. 5 ) and the PubMed-BERTScore (Fig. 6 ), with results of 0.97 vs. 0.89 and 0.95 vs. 0.68, respectively (all p = 0.0001), indicated by an asterisk and highlighted in red.

links.outcome: Readability of AI-generated reports versus accuracy trade-off for patient comprehension
links.effect: Original reports had median readability grade 13.3; readability scores correlated strongly with prompted grade (0.80-0.84), but accurate reports were only maintained down to grade 11, above the 7th-grade target.
links.quote: The readability scores exhibited a high correlation with the reading grade level, ranging from 0.80 to 0.84, indicating a very strong relationship.

links.outcome: Reading level of radiology report text relative to recommended 6th-7th grade patient level
links.effect: Original reports had median average readability 13.3 (11.8-14.8), well above the 7th-grade guideline; lowest accuracy-preserving LLM level was 11th grade.
links.quote: The overall median readability score was 13.3 (11.8–14.8).

links.outcome: Omissions, incorrect conversions and generalizations in AI-simplified reports that could reach patients unverified
links.effect: At 7th grade, inaccuracies with potential to alter management: inappropriate generalization 40% (8/20), omission 35% (7/20), incorrect conversion 35% (7/20).
links.quote: The inaccuracy patterns identified within these 20 cases were as follows: inappropriate generalization occurred in 40% (8/20), omission in 35% (7/20), and incorrect conversion in 35% (7/20).

unlisted_practices: Dual-format (simplified plus detailed) radiology reports for patients
Sentence-level traceability mapping of AI-simplified text to source report
Identifying minimum reading grade level at which LLM accuracy is preserved

links.effect: The 11th-grade level was the current lower bound; 7th-grade reports had 20% with management-altering inaccuracies.
links.quote: While 7th-grade readability remains an ethical ideal, current AI tools cannot reliably produce accurate reports below the 11th-grade level.

links.effect: At 7th grade, 20% (20/100) exhibited potential changes in patient management versus original reports.
links.quote: Among the 100 reports transformed to a 7th-grade reading level, 20% (20/100) exhibited potential changes in patient management when compared to the original reports.

screen.reason: Evaluated the impact of prompting GPT-4 across specific reading grade level constraints (grades 1-17) on clinical accuracy and potential clinical harm in patient-facing radiology reports.
